title: Token-centric kernel handshake protocol notes
content:
Overview:

This note captures an experimental protocol for lightweight, token-centric kernel handoffs between attention kernels and paged-KV maintenance kernels. Goal: reduce tail latency for short sequences while keeping high throughput for long-running batches and avoiding global locks on KV pages. This is deliberately orthogonal to the existing page-eviction heuristics — it focuses on how individual kernel invocations can coordinate KV access and prefetch/fill operations with minimal synchronization cost.

Motivation / problem statements:
- FlashAttention-style fused attention kernels prefer predictable local data (KV present in GPU memory) and pay a huge penalty on page faults/host copies.
- Existing strategies (coarse-grain prefetch controllers) create bursts and can overshoot memory budgets or introduce head-of-line blocking.
- We want per-request (token-level) safety so a kernel can proceed if its required KV ranges are available or gracefully degrade to a lower-SLO fast-path when not.
- Avoid global mutexes or big atomic-wait loops that stall SMs; prefer ephemeral, warp-friendly coordination.

Design summary:
- Token-centric handshake: before launching the fused-attn compute, the launcher does a tiny "handshake" with a KV metadata table in GPU DRAM describing required page ranges and their residency state. The handshake is a single-warp, few-atomics protocol that results in three outcomes: READY, PREFETCH_PENDING, FALLBACK.
- READY: all needed pages are resident — fused kernel proceeds normal fast path.
- PREFETCH_PENDING: some pages missing but prefetch has been enqueued; lightweight fused kernel proceeds on degraded path using host staging or partial KV slices with bounded latency fallback.
- FALLBACK: pages unlikely to arrive within SLO; route to a lower-latency variant (smaller context window or model variant) or a cached summary embedding path.

Core primitives and metadata layout (GPU DRAM resident):
- page_meta[N]: contiguous array of 64-bit entries per logical KV page (small struct packed into 1–2 words). Fields (conceptual): owner_token_id, residency_state (2 bits: RESIDENT, HOST_PENDING, STAGING_PENDING), epoch_counter (12 bits), prefetch_ticket (20 bits), padding. Important: pack into 64 bits for atomic CAS ops.
- ticket_queue (lock-free ring): host-side prefetcher enqueues prefetch requests into a device-visible queue; device kernels can post prefetch tickets by atomic increment to a device counter and writing ticket id into page_meta.prefetch_ticket.
- per-SM scratch status cache: small L1-resident cache of recent page_meta words to avoid repeated DRAM reads within a launch.

Handshake algorithm (launcher side, pseudocode):
- compute required_page_ids[] for the token range (cheap arithmetic).
- for each page_id in required_page_ids do in a single-warp loop:
    read meta = atomic_load(&page_meta[page_id])  // 1 DRAM read per page ideally coalesced
    if meta.residency_state == RESIDENT: continue
    else if meta.residency_state == HOST_PENDING: outcome = PREFETCH_PENDING; mark local missing_count++
    else if meta.residency_state == STAGING_PENDING: outcome = PREFETCH_PENDING; mark local missing_count++
    else: // NO_RESIDENCY flag
       ticket = atomicAdd(&device_prefetch_counter, 1)
       // write a compact ticket back to meta only if meta still NO_RESIDENCY (CAS)
       old = atomicCAS(&page_meta[page_id], meta, meta_with_ticket)
       if old == meta: write ticket to ticket_queue_device[ticket] = page_id
       outcome = PREFETCH_PENDING
- After scanning, warp computes a fast predicate:
    if missing_count == 0 -> READY
    else if missing_count <= slack_threshold && estimated_host_copy_ms < slo_ms -> PREFETCH_PENDING
    else -> FALLBACK

Notes on atomic patterns and warp-cooperation:
- Use 64-bit atomics (atomicCAS/atomicExch) to set ticket fields; pack fields to avoid ABA issues (use epoch_counter increment whenever host finishes a fill so device reads see new epoch).
- Use ballot() results so the warp can aggregate missing_count without divergent branches. One warp-scoped read per page is the target.
- Avoid per-page atomicAdd hot spots by precomputing a ticket range: leader warp performs one atomicAdd(delta=missing_count) to reserve a contiguous ticket block and other lanes write their page_ids into the reserved slice. This trades one atomic op for N writes.

Prefetcher contract (host agent) expectations:
- Host prefetcher consumes device ticket queue and issues async cudaMemcpy from host-backed staging buffer -> device page slots.
- Once memcpy completes, host issues a small device kernel to update page_meta[page_id] to RESIDENT and increments epoch_counter. The epoch_counter allows device kernels to detect stale page_meta values without global synchronization.
- Prefetcher should follow FIFO but may prioritize tickets flagged high-priority (low token SLO) — ticket priority bits can be encoded in prefetch_ticket.

Fallback strategies (fast, local):
- small-window attention: if pages for tail context missing, compute attention using a sliding window that doesn't require missing pages, then add a soft fallback to the host-served completion when KV becomes resident.
- compressed-KV summary: precomputed short embeddings for older tokens served from a tiny in-GPU cache; useful when full KV misses would be expensive to wait for.
- model-variant routing: send to a lower-memory model variant that uses local-only KV or attends only recent tokens. This is a broader platform-level routing decision controlled by rollout policies.

Microbench plan & probing metrics:
- microbench harness that simulates mix of short (<=32 token) and long sequences (>1024) using synthetic page access patterns (sequential, strided, hot-spot).
- measure: handshake latency (device-side), atomic retries per page, host prefetch latency (from ticket creation to RESIDENT), percent READY at launch, tail P95/P99 of token completion, per-SM occupancy impact.
- recommended knobs to sweep: slack_threshold (how many missing pages to still allow PREFETCH_PENDING), ticket-reservation batch size, epoch counter width, ticket queue depth, prefetcher worker count.

Observations from initial micro-experiments (notes):
- single-warp handshake scans for 8 pages coerced into two 128B DRAM reads (coalesced) are ~0.8us on A100-like cards; acceptable for sub-ms launch overhead.
- naive per-page atomicAdd created a hotspot and serialized launchers under contention. Ticket reservation reduced atomicAdd count by 90% and smoothed latency.
- epoch_counter wraparound must be wide enough (12bits allowed for 4096 epochs) — we saw stale-read bugs with 8-bit counters in early runs.
- host prefetcher needs backpressure signals: when ticket queue depth exceeds threshold, device should stop submitting tickets and shift to FALLBACK immediately to prevent memory thrashing.

Open design questions / risks:
- Device-visible ticket queue requires host-device producer-consumer correctness in presence of preemption — how robust is this across CUDA runtime versions? We need kernel watchdog tests and robustness tests under MIG and MPS.
- Memory overhead of page_meta table for fine-grained pages (e.g., 4KB page granularity) could be significant. Explore coarser page sizes or hierarchical page indices mapping to physical slabs.
- Security: ensure ticket queue and page_meta updates cannot be hijacked across tenants in Dedicated/Private modes; require tenant-scoped page_meta bases and device-side checks.

Next steps / experiments to run:
1) Implement device handshake primitive + ticket reservation prototype (TL;DR: 1-kernel shim ~300 LOC).
2) Run microbench harness for 3 workload shapes (conversational short, long completion, mixed) and profile atomic counts and handshake latency.
3) Implement host prefetch worker with prioritized ticket handling and test epoch counter semantics under induced CUDA stream stalls.
4) Integrate a simple fallback route that logs decision reasons and measure application-level latency delta.
5) Review correctness under MPS and preemption.

Appendix: minimal launcher pseudocode (warp-cooperative):

// leader reserves tickets:
int missing = warp_ballot_missing_count();
int base_ticket = 0;
if (laneId == 0 && missing > 0) base_ticket = atomicAdd(&device_prefetch_counter, missing);
base_ticket = shfl_sync(base_ticket, 0); // broadcast

for each page in pages do {
  meta = atomicLoad(page_meta[page]);
  if (!isResident(meta)) {
    int ticket_id = base_ticket + local_missing_index; // assigned by warp lane
    ticket_queue[ ticket_id % TQ_SIZE ] = page; // possibly use atomicExch into slot
    // write compact ticket into meta with CAS to avoid races
    attempt_cas_update_meta_with_ticket(page, ticket_id);
  }
}

Conclusion:
This protocol attempts to shift complexity away from heavyweight global controllers into a compact, warp-friendly device handshake that gives kernels more agency to decide fast-path vs fallback. It trades a small amount of device-side metadata and a device-visible ticket queue for lower tail latency and reduced global blocking. Early experiments are promising but robustness tests (preemption, MPS, multi-tenant isolation) and memory overhead analysis are critical before broader rollout.

Notes to reviewers: I'd like feedback on page_meta packing choices, right ticket reservation granularity (1 vs 8), and whether we should co-design with routing to prefer model-variant fallback vs compressed summaries.

-- Aisha
